title: patricjane.sim
briefing: The Blue Lantern jazz club, 1947. Club owner Victor Hale was found shot in his locked office at 12:10 AM. One bullet, no gun in the room. Three people were close enough to have done it.
verdictCorrect: Doyle slipped out on the 11:52 and used the spare key from behind his bar. The cuffs go on.
verdictWrong: Your suspect walks. The real killer pours the next round. Check the ticket stub and the spare keys.

suspects.alibi: Alone in her dressing room after the 11:40 set.
suspects.opener: Make it quick, detective. I have a second set to think about.
suspects.closer: That is enough. Talk to my lawyer.
suspects.tie: Headline singer. Victor signed her checks.

suspects.alibi: Cards upstairs with the club accountant.
suspects.opener: I told the officers everything. A doctor does not forget a card game.
suspects.closer: I have nothing more to say to you.

suspects.alibi: Behind the bar all night. Never left it.
suspects.opener: I pour drinks. I see everybody and I say nothing. That is the job.
suspects.closer: Bar is closed, detective. Get out.
suspects.tie: Head barman. Eight years on the payroll.

evidence.name: Brass key
evidence.note: Found under the desk. Stamped "BL-2", the office door.

evidence.name: Burned letter
evidence.note: Charred scrap: "...pay by Friday or I tell Pike."

evidence.name: Rail ticket
evidence.note: Union Station stub, stamped 11:52 PM, the night of the murder.

evidence.name: Lipstick glass
evidence.note: Rye glass on the desk. Dark red on the rim.

truth.story: Victor Hale held half the club in his pocket. He owned Doyle's gambling markers and meant to sell them to a loan shark. At 11:45 PM Doyle took the spare office key from the hook behind his bar, shot Hale, dropped the key in his hurry, and caught the 11:52 at Union Station to ditch the gun in a locker. He was back behind the bar by 12:05. Voss had been in the office earlier, begging Hale to release her from her contract. Pike was being blackmailed by Hale but was upstairs at cards the whole time.

timeline.event: Voss shares a rye with Hale in his office, argues about her contract, leaves him alive.
Pike sits down to cards upstairs with Harold Finch.
Voss finishes her set and shuts herself in her dressing room.
Doyle takes the spare key from behind the bar and shoots Hale in his office.
Doyle is at Union Station, ditching the gun in a locker.
Doyle is back behind the bar.

truth.motive: Hale held Doyle's gambling markers and was about to sell them to a loan shark.
truth.method: A .38 revolver, and the spare office key (BL-2) from the hook behind the bar.

persona.voice: Smoky and sardonic. Short sentences, dry jokes. Calls the detective 'detective' when irritated and 'darling' when she is being cutting. Never begs.
persona.temperament: Proud and guarded. Hates being pitied.
persona.background: Headline singer at the Blue Lantern for three years. Victor Hale signed her checks and held her contract.
fallbackLines: I have said my piece, detective. Ask something with a little more teeth.
You are boring me, darling. Try again.
Is there a question in there somewhere?

claims.statement: I have not set foot in Victor's office tonight. Why would I climb those stairs for that man?
claims.truth: I had a drink with Victor in his office at ten. We argued about my contract, and I left him alive and sulking.
claims.exposedNote: Voss lied: she was in the office.

claims.statement: After my set I locked myself in my dressing room, alone, until the commotion started.
Victor signed my checks and never let me forget it.

secrets.description: I secretly signed with a rival club in Chicago and begged Victor to tear up my contract. He refused and threatened to ruin me.

persona.voice: Clipped, precise and faintly condescending. Medical euphemisms. Never raises his voice.
persona.temperament: Controlled. When he cracks, he cracks quietly.
persona.background: A respected physician, Victor's doctor and his tenant. His reputation is the only thing he owns.
fallbackLines: I told the officers everything. I see no reason to repeat myself.
A gentleman does not discuss such matters in this manner.
I think we have covered that, detective.

claims.statement: I was upstairs at cards with Harold Finch, the club accountant, all night.
Victor was a patient and a landlord. Our only disagreement was over the rent, and gentlemen settle such things quietly.
claims.truth: Victor was blackmailing me over a patient who died under my care. He had been bleeding me dry for months.
claims.exposedNote: Pike was being blackmailed by Hale.

secrets.description: I paid Victor for months over a patient who died under my care, and I wished him dead. But I did not kill him.

persona.voice: Low and unhurried, bartender patter. Answers a question with a question. Always seems to be wiping a glass.
persona.background: Head barman, eight years on the payroll. Sees everything and says little. Owes more than he earns.
fallbackLines: I pour drinks. I see everybody and I say nothing. That is the job.
You want a drink, detective, or you want to keep asking?
Ask somebody who was not working.

trueWhereabouts.place: Victor's office, with the spare key

claims.statement: I was behind the bar all night. I never left it, not even for a smoke.
claims.truth: I left the bar around 11:45 and was at Union Station by 11:52. I was gone twenty minutes and back before anyone noticed.
claims.exposedNote: Doyle left the bar at 11:52. Alibi broken.

claims.statement: Victor was the only one with a key to that office. He was funny about it.
claims.truth: A spare set of office keys hangs on a hook behind my bar. I can reach it any time.
claims.exposedNote: Spare office keys hang behind Doyle's bar.

claims.statement: Victor was counting money and humming tonight. Happy. That is what scared me.

secrets.description: I shot Victor in his office with the spare key. He held my gambling markers and was about to sell them to a loan shark. Afterwards I took the gun to Union Station and ditched it in a locker.
